accept.reason: Fills a real need: SWE-Bench Verified is near saturation (>70% reported) while the strongest agents resolve at most 23.3% here, leaving headroom to track progress
accept.location: Abstract; Section 1 ('In the next 6 - 12 months, there will be diminishing feedback from SWE-Bench-Verified'); Table 1 (GPT-5 23.3)

accept.reason: A three-tier access design for contamination resistance: copyleft-licensed public and held-out sets plus a private commercial set, which the paper argues has not been applied systematically to a research benchmark
accept.location: Section 1 ('exclusively selecting repositories distributed under strong copyleft licenses (GPL)'); Section 3.1; Section 3.3

accept.reason: Tasks are larger than in SWE-Bench Verified: reference solutions average 107.4 lines across 4.1 files, every task changes at least 10 lines
accept.location: Section 1 ('On average, the reference solutions span 107.4 lines of code across 4.1 files'); Figure 3 caption

accept.reason: Human augmentation adds a problem statement, requirements and an interface specification so that agents are not failed for misnaming functions or missing information (fewer false negatives)
accept.location: Section 3.2 (Requirements, Interface); Section 4.2; Appendix A.2-A.3; Table 4

accept.reason: Environment and test verification: Dockerfiles built by professional engineers, tests run 3 times to remove flaky tests, human filtering of irrelevant or too-broad fail2pass tests
accept.location: Section 3.2 ('we run each set of tests 3 times'); Section 4.3

accept.reason: Uniform evaluation protocol: one scaffold (SWE-Agent), the same prompt, a 200-turn cap and a fixed model-version date for all seven models
accept.location: Section 5 ('We use the same prompt for all models'; 'latest versions as of September 18th, 2025')

accept.reason: A private commercial set gives an enterprise-code evaluation that public benchmarks cannot offer, and the paper reports results on it (best 17.8%)
Diagnostic analyses beyond a leaderboard: breakdowns by language and repository and a trajectory failure-mode taxonomy, with the judge prompt released
accept.location: Section 6.1; Figure 4; Section 6.2; Table 3; Appendix B.1

accept.reason: The public set (731 tasks) is released with pre-built Docker images and evaluation code, and the agent-judge prompt is given
accept.location: Section 3.3 ('We release 731 instances openly on HuggingFace'); Section 3.2 ('All environments will be released as pre-built docker images'); data/code links on p.1

accept.reason: Breadth: 41 actively maintained repositories across consumer apps, B2B services and developer tools, with a per-repository cap to prevent one repo dominating
accept.location: Abstract; Section 1 ('strict cap of 100 instances'); Section 3.1

accept.reason: The task format is clearly specified and illustrated with a full worked instance and an original-vs-rewritten issue comparison
Candid limitations: language coverage, dependence on test suites, and the reduced ambiguity introduced by augmentation are acknowledged
A held-out set from separate repositories is retained to detect future overfitting to the public set
accept.location: Section 3.3 ('We keep this set private to test for overfitting in the future')

accept.reason: Multi-language coverage (Python, Go, JavaScript, TypeScript) beyond the Python-only SWE-bench, with per-language results

reject.reason: The contamination-resistance claim is never tested. The 'legal barriers' of GPL are asserted, not shown; no memorization probe, no commit-date vs training-cutoff analysis, and the held-out set built for this purpose is never evaluated
reject.location: Section 3.1 ('creates legal barriers to their inclusion in commercial training corpora'); Section 5 ('we keep the private set held-out for future analysis'); Abstract ('contamination-resistant testbed')
reject.fix: Evaluate the held-out set and compare with the public set; add a commit-date vs cutoff analysis or a memorization probe; or soften to 'designed to reduce contamination'. Cost: a few agent runs (days of API budget)

reject.reason: Single run Pass@1 without confidence intervals. With N=731 the binomial standard error near 23% is about 1.6 points, so GPT-5 (23.3) vs Opus 4.1 (22.7) is not separable, yet the abstract calls GPT-5 'the highest score to date'
reject.location: Table 1; Abstract ('GPT-5 achieving the highest score to date at 23.3%'); derived SE = sqrt(0.233*0.767/731) = 1.56 pp
reject.fix: Report binomial or bootstrap 95% CIs (free from existing runs) and, ideally, 3 runs for the top models; soften ranking claims. Cost: none to moderate

reject.reason: Results rest on one scaffold with a 200-turn cap. The scaffold-model fit visibly drives outcomes (GPT-5 does not submit on 63.1% of its failures, 97.6% of those tool-use errors), and Agentless is dismissed without numbers
reject.location: Section 5 ('we find that Agentless has difficulty in multi-file editing'; 'maximum of 200 turns'); Table 3 (GPT-5 Not-Submitted 63.1%, Tool-Use 97.6%)
reject.fix: Report the Agentless numbers already run; add a second agent scaffold (e.g., OpenHands) for the top models; report turn-limit sensitivity. Cost: moderate API budget

reject.reason: The headline contrast with '>70% on SWE-Bench Verified' is not a controlled comparison: Verified numbers come from vendor reports with other scaffolds, not the paper's SWE-Agent configuration, so the difficulty gap is confounded with scaffold and settings
reject.location: Figure 2 caption ('score >70% of SWE-Bench Verified but less than 25%'); Section 1 ('over 70% pass rate on SWE-Bench-Verified [15]')
reject.fix: Run the same SWE-Agent configuration on SWE-Bench Verified for the same models. Cost: low-moderate API budget

reject.reason: Error (E1): Table 3 trajectory counts exceed the size of the set analysed. Section 6.2 filters 'to only unresolved instances' of the public set (N=731), but Opus 4.1 has 681+239=920 classified failures and Gemini 915; with a 22.7% resolve rate Opus should have about 565 unresolved
reject.location: Table 3 (Opus 4.1 (681), (239); Gemini (491), (424)); Section 6.2 ('programmatically filter to only unresolved instances'); Table 1 (N=731). Recomputed: 731 x (1-0.227) = 565
reject.fix: Explain what the denominators are (multiple runs? commercial set? resolved trajectories?) and recompute Table 3 on the stated population. Cost: low

reject.reason: Error (E1): 'Qwen 3 32B ... exhibits the highest tool error rate (42.0%)' does not match Table 3: Qwen's tool-use share of all failures is 51.3% x 86.0% = 44.1%, and GPT-5's is 63.1% x 97.6% = 61.6%
reject.location: Section 6.2 ('exhibits the highest tool error rate (42.0%)'); Table 3. Recomputed from table percentages and counts (349/792 = 44.1%)
reject.fix: Correct the number and the ranking. Cost: trivial

reject.reason: Error (E1): the text contradicts Table 1: 'Claude 4 Sonnet also achieves a 16.3% resolve rate' (Table 1: 17.6) and GPT-4o '3.9%' (Table 1: 4.9); Qwen-3 32B is called 'DeepSeek Qwen-3 32B'
reject.location: Section 5 Results ('also achieves a 16.3% resolve rate'; 'at 3.4% and 3.9% respectively'); Table 1
reject.fix: Align text and table. Cost: trivial

reject.reason: Error (E5, claim distortion): the introduction says smaller models such as Qwen 3 32B 'more frequently fail due to issues in syntax and formatting', but by Table 3 syntax errors are 24.2% of Opus 4.1 failures vs 23.2% of Qwen's; the text also reads 24.2% syntax errors as 'strong technical execution'
reject.location: Section 1 ('smaller models (e.g., Qwen 3 32B) more frequently fail due to issues in syntax and formatting'); Section 6.2 ('suggesting strong technical execution'); Table 3 (Opus 74.0% x 32.7% = 24.2%; Qwen 48.7% x 47.7% = 23.2%)
reject.fix: Restate the failure-mode conclusions to match Table 3 (or report rates on a common denominator). Cost: low

reject.reason: The LLM-judge failure analysis is not validated on this benchmark: GPT-5 judges its own and its competitors' trajectories, agreement with humans is borrowed from another paper (87%), the '20 turns' human comparison gives no numbers, and 'Other' absorbs 63.4% of Sonnet 4's submitted failures
reject.location: Section 6.2 ('utilizing GPT-5 as the judge'; 'demonstrate 87% alignment'; 'We determined 20 turns to have the highest correspondence'); Table 3 (Sonnet 4 Other 63.4%)
reject.fix: Report human-judge agreement (kappa) on a labelled sample for each model, use a second judge to check self-preference, refine the 'Other' bucket. Cost: a few annotator-days

reject.reason: The 'long-horizon' framing (title) and 'tasks that may require hours to days for a professional software engineer' are not operationalized: no human solve-time estimates, no agent trajectory-length or turn statistics; only lines and files changed are measured
reject.location: Title; Abstract ('may require hours to days for a professional software engineer to complete'); Section 1; Figure 3 caption
reject.fix: Report annotator time estimates or measured human solve times on a sample, and trajectory length/turn distributions; otherwise drop 'long-horizon'. Cost: low-moderate

reject.reason: The human-written requirements and interface are derived from the tests and gold patch, so the benchmark measures implementing a precise specification rather than resolving an issue; the paper asserts they 'don’t leak solutions' but runs no ablation without requirements/interface
reject.location: Section 3.2 ('These requirements are grounded on the unit tests'); Appendix A.2 ('Requirements never include specific code implementation and don’t leak solutions'); Section 5 Issue Ambiguity; Section 7.1 Reduction in Ambiguity
reject.fix: Ablate on the public set: problem statement only vs + requirements vs + interface; audit a sample of requirements for solution leakage. Cost: moderate API budget plus annotation

reject.reason: Quality control of the human pipeline is unreported: number and expertise of annotators, agreement, how many candidate tasks/tests were dropped at each stage, and whether any human independently solved tasks; so 'All tasks are human-verified ... to ensure resolvability' is unsupported
reject.location: Abstract ('All tasks are human-verified and augmented with sufficient context to ensure resolvability'); Sections 4.2-4.3 (no counts or agreement); not stated after search
reject.fix: Add a pipeline funnel table (candidates -> kept at each stage), annotator details, agreement, and a human-solvability check on a sample. Cost: low for reporting, moderate for a solvability study

reject.reason: The public-vs-commercial gap is attributed to 'greater complexity of enterprise codebases' without any complexity statistics for the commercial set; the sets differ in repositories, languages and tasks per repository, and model order changes (Sonnet 4: 17.6 -> 9.1)
reject.location: Section 1 ('underscoring the greater complexity of enterprise codebases'); Section 5; Tables 1-2
reject.fix: Report LOC, files, language mix and repo sizes for the commercial set and compare at matched task size. Cost: low

reject.reason: Error (E6): the per-repository count claim does not hold for the commercial set: 'Each repository contributes between 50 and 100 instances' but 276 commercial tasks over 18 repositories average 15.3 per repository; Section 3.1 also says '50-100+' against the 'strict cap of 100'
reject.location: Section 1 ('Each repository contributes between 50 and 100 instances, with a strict cap of 100'); Section 3.1 ('contribute 50-100+ instances'); Abstract (18 commercial repositories); Section 3.3 (276 problems). Recomputed 276/18 = 15.3
reject.fix: State the rule per subset and report per-repo counts. Cost: trivial

reject.reason: Two of three subsets are private: commercial results cannot be reproduced by others, and no statistics of the held-out or commercial sets are given
reject.location: Section 3.3; Section 5 ('For all analysis, we use the public set')
reject.fix: Publish aggregate statistics of both private sets and a submission protocol for third-party evaluation. Cost: low

reject.reason: Evaluation details needed to reproduce Table 1 are missing: exact model identifiers, decoding temperature, context and token/cost budgets, how syntax-parsed tool use works for open-weight models, and per-run cost; SWE-Smith-32B is used without a citation
reject.location: Section 5 Evaluation settings ('All models use the latest versions as of September 18th, 2025'; 'we use syntax parsing to enable tool-use'); Table 1 (SWE-Smith-32B); reference list (no SWE-smith entry)
reject.fix: Add a configuration table per model and release run configs and trajectories. Cost: low

reject.reason: Dataset statistics are thin and partly unclear: which subset the 107.4 LOC / 4.1 files average covers is not stated, and 'over 100 tasks demand more than 100 lines' sits oddly with a mean of 107.4 unless the tail is heavy; distributions exist only in Figure 3 (not readable here)
reject.location: Section 1 ('over 100 tasks demand more than 100 lines of modification'); Figure 3 caption ('Distributions in the public set')
reject.fix: Give a statistics table per subset (median/IQR LOC, files, hunks, tests) in text. Cost: trivial

reject.reason: Minor inconsistencies: 'exclude trivial edits (1-10 lines)' vs 'at least 10 lines'; the Figure 4 caption mentions '10+ files and 500+ LOC' categories not described in the text; Table 3 columns do not map one-to-one onto the 10 judge categories in Appendix B.1 (e.g., 'endless file reading' in the text)
reject.location: Section 1; Figure 4 caption; Table 3; Section 6.2 ('endless file reading behaviors (17.0%)'); Appendix B.1 category list
reject.fix: Fix wording and add a category mapping. Cost: trivial

reject.reason: Citation errors (E7): the abstract's 'best practices of SWE-Bench [25]' points to 'Swe-bench goes live!'; 'social media posts [1, 25]' points to two arXiv papers
reject.location: Abstract ('builds upon the best practices of SWE-Bench [25]'); Section 1 ('social media posts [1, 25]'); References [1], [13], [25]
reject.fix: Correct the reference numbers. Cost: trivial

reject.reason: The construction is a refinement of the SWE-bench recipe: the commit-pair / fail2pass sourcing (Section 4.1) follows SWE-bench [13], human verification follows SWE-Bench Verified [15], multi-language follows Multi-SWE-bench [24], contamination freshness is addressed by SWE-bench-Live [25]; the new parts are copyleft/commercial sourcing and requirements/interface augmentation
reject.location: Section 4.1; Section 3.1 ('Similar to SWE-Bench Verified'); Section 2.1; Section 1 ('to the best of our knowledge, this work is the first')
reject.fix: Position the delta explicitly with a comparison table against SWE-bench, Verified, Multi-SWE-bench, SWE-bench-Live (size, languages, LOC, files, contamination strategy). Cost: low

reject.reason: Related work omits closely related benchmarks and contamination strategies, e.g., freelance-task SWE evaluation (Miserendino et al., 'SWE-Lancer: Can Frontier LLMs Earn $1 Million from Real-World Freelance Software Engineering?', 2025), executable training environments (Pan et al., 'Training Software Engineering Agents and Verifiers with SWE-Gym', 2024; Yang et al., 'SWE-smith: Scaling Data for Software Engineering Agents', 2025), and time-based contamination control (Jain et al., 'LiveCodeBench: Holistic and Contamination Free Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code', 2024)
reject.location: Section 2.1-2.2 (none of these discussed)
reject.fix: Add and position these works. Cost: trivial

reject.reason: Sourcing and consent of commercial code are described inconsistently and incompletely: 'purchased their engineering repos' (Section 3.1) vs 'formal partnership agreements' (Abstract) vs internal assets incl. acquired companies and employee-founded startups (Section 4.1); no statement on secrets/PII scrubbing, licence terms of the GPL derivative, or annotator compensation
reject.location: Abstract; Section 3.1 ('we contacted the company and purchased their engineering repos'); Section 4.1 ('including companies acquired through mergers and acquisitions')
reject.fix: Add a data statement: sourcing agreements, PII/secret scrubbing, licences, annotator pay; disclose any affiliation of commercial-set sources. Cost: low

reject.reason: Language coverage is narrow for a benchmark framed as 'diverse': Python, Go, JavaScript, TypeScript only; Java, C++, Rust absent (acknowledged)
reject.location: Section 7.1 ('some widely-used languages like Java, C++, and Rust are underrepresented'); Abstract ('diverse set of 41 actively maintained repositories')
reject.fix: Scope the claim; plan expansion. Cost: none for wording

reject.reason: Model coverage is thin for a benchmark paper: only two open-weight models (Qwen-3 32B, SWE-Smith-32B), no strong open coding agents; no analysis of resolve rate vs task size in text
reject.location: Table 1; Section 6.1; Figure 4 caption
reject.fix: Add 2-3 strong open-weight coding models and a resolve-rate vs LOC/files plot. Cost: moderate GPU budget

reject.reason: Test validity is not measured in either direction: no estimate of false negatives (valid alternative solutions failing the tests; acknowledged) and no audit of resolved patches for false positives passing weak tests
reject.location: Section 7.1 Dependency on Test Suite; Section 4.3; not stated after search
reject.fix: Manually audit a sample of resolved and unresolved patches per model and report FP/FN rates. Cost: a few engineer-days

reject.reason: Figure 1's caption lists 'difficulty filtering', but Section 4 describes only size-based exclusion; if tasks were also filtered by model failure, the low resolve rates would be partly by construction
reject.location: Figure 1 caption ('difficulty filtering'); Section 1 ('we exclude trivial edits (1-10 lines of code)'); Section 3.1 ('problems are naturally challenging')

reject.location: Section 1 ('state-of-the-art agents have reported over 70% pass rate on SWE-Bench-Verified [15]'); Figure 2 caption; Reference [15] ('OpenAI, 2024')
